A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DistDF. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments, component ablations, conditional-correlation analysis, sensitivity studies and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds architecture comparisons, autoregressive and probabilistic evaluations, and convergence measurements.

M1.justification: DistDF retains joint history–future concatenation, Bures–Wasserstein mean/covariance matching and combination with MSE. Renaming alpha to gamma and correcting Algorithm 1's forecast concatenation make the presentation consistent with v1's existing prose. No new DistDF component is specified for the added evaluations.

E1.justification: The underlying datasets remain unchanged, including Traffic and PEMS retained in v2 Table 6. However, Appendix D.9/Table 10 adds probabilistic forecasting on ETTm1 and Weather, substantially extending task coverage beyond v1's point-forecast evaluations. Additional multiscale architectures do not themselves constitute new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with TQNet, D3U, TimeMixer and SCINet, each tested with and without DistDF in Tables 8, 10 and 11. The original architecture and learning-objective comparator sets remain. Earlier citations to some added models did not constitute evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces autoregressive evaluation in Table 9 and probabilistic evaluation using CRPS and CRPSsum alongside MSE/MAE in Table 10. These additions substantially broaden testing procedures and metrics, while retaining history length 96 and the four standard forecast horizons. Detailed rollout and probabilistic-sampling procedures are not supplied.

E4.justification: Appendix D.7/Figure 8 adds an optimization diagnostic tracking training and validation Bures–Wasserstein discrepancy alongside validation MAE/MSE for ETTm1, ETTh1 and ECL. Existing component ablations, discrepancy comparisons, sensitivity studies, forecast examples and runtime analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean and standard deviation over seeds 2021–2025 in v1 Table 11/v2 Table 13, and retain 50% confidence intervals in Figures 3 and 6. No additional run-count, significance-test or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Matched original tables retain their numerical results. v2 nevertheless adds substantial results in Tables 8–11 and Figure 8. For example, new Table 10 reports Weather average CRPSsum of 0.275 for D3U and 0.255 with DistDF. These are additional comparisons under newly evaluated settings, not improvements over v1's corresponding scores.

T1.justification: The central bias formula, alignment theorem, Gaussian Bures–Wasserstein formula and proof arguments remain. Appendix B removes v1's explicit definition relating the p-Wasserstein distance to the pth root of optimal transport cost, constituting a limited removal of mathematical content.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that likelihood objectives suffer autocorrelation bias, propose tractable joint-distribution alignment, and claim improvements across forecasting models. Rephrasing performance claims and adding supporting experiments do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: The conclusion replaces suggestions about other application domains and transformed-domain discrepancies with a concrete limitation: matching means and covariances cannot fully characterize non-Gaussian distributions. New Appendix D.7 also interprets decreasing BW discrepancy as supporting improved validation accuracy, although its claim of monotonic decrease exceeds the fluctuating trajectories shown.

D1.justification: v2 removes v1's dataset-description table and substantial reproduction details, including split sample counts, sampling descriptions, the explicit learning-rate grid and validation-MSE selection rule, and the OLS-residual recipe for partial correlations. Some optimizer and hardware information moves into Section 4.1. The code pointer changes from an anonymous repository to GitHub; accessibility was not independently verified.

R1.justification: Literature coverage is substantially revised, adding joint-distribution optimal transport by Courty et al. (2017a), D3U, distribution-aware alignment by Hu et al. (2026), and numerous recent forecasting and graph-model works. Several earlier survey, dataset-source and policy-optimization references disappear. The central positioning against FreDF and Time-o1 remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, formulation, implementation and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Notation is standardized, Section 4 foregrounds learning-objective comparisons, and architecture benchmarking shifts to the appendix. Reproduction material is substantially condensed, appendix sections are reorganized, and the reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–11 and convergence Figure 8, removes the standalone benchmark-summary and dataset-description tables, and extensively relocates retained displays. Algorithm 1 becomes full-width, Figure 2 reverses paired forecast-panel order, and Figure 3 regroups panel labels. The removed benchmark summary's results survive in the full appendix table.

improvement.justification: The added probabilistic, autoregressive and architecture evaluations provide useful evidence about applicability beyond the original experiments, while the explicit non-Gaussian limitation improves qualification of the claims. The central method and original results remain stable. The overall gain is limited by removal of detailed reproduction information, sparse explanations of the new evaluation procedures, and overstated convergence language.
